newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil traders say Iraq crude price attractive.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil traders say Iraq crude price attractive.

text.p: Japanese crude oil traders said on Friday they are keen to buy Iraqi crude as the price has been set at competitive levels.
But they said they were in no hurry to buy, having covered the bulk of their immediate requirements.

"We are very interested in buying Iraqi crude, especially as other Middle Eastern crudes in the spot market have been fetching high premiums this year," said a crude oil trader with a leading refiner.
"But we are in no hurry to buy, as most of our demand for December and January cargoes has been covered," he said.
Traders said Japanese buying of Iraqi crude is expected to emerge from February-loading cargoes, possibly as early as January cargoes, displacing similar Iranian, Oman and Dubai grades.
Before the 1991 Gulf War that followed Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, Japan was a major importer of Iraqi crude.
Most traders consider Basrah Light crude to be competitive price-wise, as the price is lower than the similar Saudi Arabian Light crude.
SOMO, Iraq's state oil firm, has set the December price formula of Basrah Light crude to Asian buyers at a premium of 20 cents to the average of Oman and Dubai quotations.
December-loading Saudi Arabian Light crude to East Asia is priced at 75 cents above the average of Oman and Dubai quotations.

Premiums of Middle Eastern crudes in the Asian spot market have maintained levels above their official selling price this year, partly because of increased demand due to the start-up of new refineries in the region, traders said.
Other than the price, Japanese refiners said they like the quality of Iraqi crude.
"We are interested in buying Iraqi crude because our evaluation of the quality of Iraqi crude is very high," a trader with another refiner said.
Although traders were upbeat about buying Iraqi crude, they said shipping may prove to be an obstacle to imports.

The Ship Owners Labour Relations Agency said the southern Iraqi port of Mina al-Bakr, from which crude exports to Asia are due to leave, has areas surrounding it that are dangerous as a result of buried mines.
"Unless proven safe, we will not allow Japanese sailors to sail to Mina al-Bakr," an agency official said.
